lines.text: Do you know how lightning works? A single bolt can heat the air to about thirty thousand degrees. Hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Inside a storm cloud, strong winds toss ice crystals and soft hail called graupel up and down. They crash into each other millions of times.
Every collision swaps a little charge. Light crystals carry positive charge to the top. Heavier graupel drags negative charge to the bottom.
When the charge gets strong enough, an invisible channel called a stepped leader zigzags down from the cloud, a few dozen meters at a time.
As it gets close, the ground answers. Tall things like trees and towers send up streamers to meet it.
They connect, and a huge current races back up the channel. That's the flash you see. It's over in a fraction of a second.
The air heats so fast it explodes outward. That shock wave is thunder.
Light reaches you almost instantly, sound doesn't. Count the seconds between the flash and the thunder, divide by three, and that's roughly how many kilometers away it struck.
